nodes.body: Gallowmere arrives out of the freezing rain looking like a decision somebody regretted immediately: a leaning stockade, a Warden's tower with a lamp burning at the wrong hour, and a muster yard already crowded with companies who got here first. Dellach counts the competition under his breath and does not like the arithmetic. Nyre reads the notice at the gate twice, which is her way of disagreeing with it. Kettle, who has not said a useful word since the hill came in sight, says nothing at all.

choices.label: Report to the Warden-Marshal at once.
Take the company into the Broken Wheel first.
Walk the muster yard and see who else is hiring.
Let Nyre take you to the Ledger counting room.
Ask Kettle what she is not saying about the moor.

nodes.body: Warden-Marshal Ansel Redd lays the commission out without decoration. The winter tax-iron of the Kar Duhn garrison never came down the road, and neither did the garrison. Sixty crowns for the iron and the pay-ledger both, paid on delivery, and no Warden will set foot past the barrow gate with you. He says the last part before you can ask it.

choices.label: Ask what actually happened to the garrison.
Press him for better terms before you sign.
Sign it as written and be done.

nodes.body: His answer is thin and he knows it. Two relief patrols went up to the barrow gate; the first turned back for reasons the sergeant could not commit to paper, and the second came home nine men short. The vault door, both patrols agreed, was standing open exactly a hand's width, and neither of them could say who had opened it.

choices.label: Press him for better terms now that you know.
Sign anyway; the coin is the coin.

nodes.body: The haggle happens in a cold office with the shutters banging, and Redd has no more coin anywhere in his district. What he has instead is a charter: a stamped writ of salvage that would make the Ninth Sword a name on a Warden's list instead of a hired knife. He will part with it only if you drop the hazard pay entirely.

choices.label: Take the charter and drop the hazard pay.
Take the coin; charters do not feed anyone.
Refuse the whole insult and ride south.

nodes.body: The writ is stamped, sanded, and entered in the tower book by a clerk who spells your company's name correctly on the second attempt. Dellach says nothing whatsoever and stands a little straighter, while Nyre notes in her own book precisely what the arrangement has cost.

choices.label: Gather the company.

nodes.body: The contract is signed with the Marshal's seal still warm, and then he adds his last condition quietly, as though it were an afterthought. Bring back the pay-ledger even if the iron is beyond you. The ledger is what his own account will be measured against, and he would rather be measured accurately.

choices.label: Ask him for a guide across the moor.
Ask to read the garrison's last dispatch.
Go and gather your company.

nodes.body: The only guide willing to take the moor road is Bram Sull, a fen-runner with a drinker's hands, who wants a full share and swears he has walked the dykes blind in fog. Kettle looks at him the way you look at weather coming in from the west, and does not offer an opinion aloud.

choices.label: Hire him out of the advance.
Refuse; Kettle knows the moor better than she admits.

nodes.body: Bram is hired out of the advance and has spent a third of his share before the horses are stabled. Dellach considers him unimpressive and Kettle considers him a liability, so the company is five now, and one of the five is a stranger who talks.

choices.label: Gather the company.

nodes.body: The garrison's last dispatch is water-stained and written in a clerk's failing hand: routine counts, routine weather, routine complaints about the oil ration. Then, at the bottom, in the same failing hand and pressed much harder, a line that is not routine in any way. The ninth hand is missing and the door will not hold at eight.

choices.label: Take that with you and gather the company.

nodes.body: The Broken Wheel is peat smoke and wet wool and three companies drinking on other people's commissions. A charcoal burner at the end of the bench is telling anyone who will listen about lamps that move across the moor in single file. Over by the fire, one of Corrow's Rooks has begun measuring Dellach for a joke he intends to tell loudly.

choices.label: Buy the room a round and listen.
Corner the charcoal burner about the lamps.
Get between Dellach and the Rooks bravo.
Take the company upstairs; sleep is worth more.

nodes.body: A round bought for the room loosens it considerably. The Kar Duhn garrison paid its own wages nine times over on paper, according to a man who used to cart their flour. A Ledger factor came up from the south twice this autumn, which nobody can explain. And nobody in Gallowmere, at any price, will take a contract past the barrow gate.

choices.label: Follow up the lamps story.
You have heard enough for one night.

nodes.body: Sober enough to be precise, the charcoal burner is extremely precise. Lamps in a file of nine, always nine, moving along the old dwarf road at the same hour of the night. They stop at the barrow gate and wait there a while, as though somebody inside has to count them in before they are permitted to pass.

choices.label: Pay him for the whole story, slowly.
Write him off as drink and firelight.
Have him walk you out to see the lamps tonight.

nodes.body: The remainder costs two coppers. The lamps have come every ninth night since midsummer, as regular as a tax collector, and his brother followed them once out of curiosity and drink. What came back to the charcoal hut four days later was his brother's coat, folded neatly, with every button cut off.

choices.label: Let him go and gather the company.

nodes.body: Corrow's bravo has decided the Ninth Sword is a joke worth telling at volume, and he is most of the way through the second telling. Dellach's hand is already flat on the table, which is invariably how it begins with him, and the room has gone quiet enough to hear the fire working.

choices.label: Let Dellach settle it with fists.
Pull rank and buy the man's drink.
Draw steel in a Warden town.

nodes.body: It takes three exchanges. The bravo ends up folded over a bench with his opinion of your company substantially revised, and the room's opinion of the Rooks revised in the other direction. Dellach's knuckles are split to the bone. Nyre binds the hand without one word of comment, which is worse than comment.

choices.label: Get the company upstairs before it starts again.

nodes.body: A bought drink, a hard smile, and the bravo backs off describing the whole business as professional courtesy. Dellach believes you spent coin on nothing at all; Kettle believes you bought the only thing in Gallowmere actually worth having, which is one quiet night before the moor.

choices.label: Take the stairs and the quiet night.

nodes.body: One night in a real bed above a warm floor, with boots off and the door barred, and the company sleeps like paid soldiers instead of hunted ones. You wake before the bell and can feel the difference in your hands.

choices.label: Gather the company at first light.

nodes.body: The muster yard in the rain: two companies loading out, the Rooks' banner pitched over the only dry ground, and a scatter of loose hands hoping for a fourth-share. One of them is a woman in a salt-stained coat, sitting on a crate, reading the warding sigils off a wagon axle as though they were a bill of lading.

choices.label: Talk to the woman reading sigils.
Hire the two spear-brothers who ask for little.
Cross the yard to the Rooks banner.
Hire nobody; four mouths is enough.

nodes.body: Ilsabet Crane, hedge-thaumaturge, glass and salt and one badly burned sleeve. She reads the wagon's warding aloud, corrects it, and then tells you plainly what nobody in the tower would say: whatever emptied Kar Duhn was let in rather than broken in. The marks on the relief patrol's shields were made from the inside.

choices.label: Take her on at a full share.
Offer her half a share and see if she takes it.

nodes.body: A full share, agreed with a handshake she does not release until you meet her eye. She owns exactly one crate, and everything in it is written on rather than made of anything, and Kettle helps her carry it up without being asked, which from Kettle is a formal endorsement.

choices.label: Gather the company.

nodes.body: Half a share, taken with a shrug that costs you something you cannot price yet. She comes, and she works, and she keeps roughly one hand's worth of what she knows in reserve, which is exactly the arrangement you paid for.

choices.label: Gather the company.

nodes.body: The spear-brothers are Odd and Sten, cheap and cheerful and entirely untested, and they ask about the coin twice and about the moor not once. Dellach hires them regardless, on the reasonable grounds that a shield wall of two men is not a shield wall at all.

choices.label: Gather the company.

nodes.body: Captain Vasse Corrow of the Rooks is dry under an oiled awning with a cup in her hand, and she offers to buy your commission outright for forty crowns, which she describes as mercy. She has been to the barrow gate herself. She will not say what turned her around, and she does not pretend that nothing did.

choices.label: Refuse, and drink with her long enough to learn why.
Take the forty crowns and live.

nodes.body: Corrow drinks steadily and talks around the edges of it. Her scout went in at the gate and came out wrong, counting under her breath, in nines. She would not stop counting for anything, food included, and she died of it eleven days later in a Ledger hospice with the count still going.

choices.label: Leave her the awning and gather your company.

nodes.body: The Ledger counting room is warm as a church and considerably quieter, and Factor Halloway keeps the frontier's debts in a hand like engraving. Nyre's order and his are the same order, which is precisely why she does not trust him. He offers hot wine and asks after the company's health as if he already knew the answer.

choices.label: Have Nyre read the garrison's pay account.
Borrow against the commission for better kit.
Hear out the contract Halloway would rather offer.
Leave; Ledger business is her business.

nodes.body: Nyre reads the garrison's pay account aloud in the flat voice she reserves for bad news. The Kar Duhn garrison drew its winter pay nine times in nine years, and every single draw was signed by a different hand. The ninth signature, at the bottom of the final page, is not a name at all but a mark.

choices.label: Take that with you.

nodes.body: Credit against the commission, spent properly: oil, dry powder, two lamps with clean wicks, a new haft for Dellach's poleaxe, and enough salt for Ilsabet to work with. The debt settles in behind the company like a second contract, and this one has interest.

choices.label: Load out and gather the company.

nodes.body: Halloway's better offer is laid out with what appears to be genuine kindness. Forget the iron entirely, bring him the pay-ledger alone, and the Ledger will carry the Ninth Sword's debts for nine years, term for term and hand for hand. He uses the word nine twice while explaining it.

choices.label: Sign what Halloway is actually offering.
Refuse, and note that he used the word nine.

nodes.body: Kettle is up on the rampart with her back to the moor, lying badly about why she took this particular contract. She was born in the fens directly under that hill, and she has not said the words Kar Duhn once since Gallowmere came into view. She is saying them now only because you asked a second time.

choices.label: Press her, gently, until she says it.
Let her keep it; everyone is owed one silence.
Tell the Marshal she is holding something back.

nodes.body: The truth comes out in pieces, none of them comfortable. She went under the hill at eleven years old with her father's crew, who were paid in silence and salt to carry crates down the stair and nothing at all back up. She is the only member of that crew still walking around above ground.

choices.label: Ask what the crews sang down there.
That is enough for tonight.

nodes.body: The crews had a counting rhyme for the stair, and she recites it without any expression whatsoever, the way you recite something you have deliberately not thought about for twenty years. Nine hands on the iron, nine irons in the door. Eight to hold it shut, and the ninth to keep the score.

choices.label: Sit with that a while, then gather the company.

nodes.body: The Marshal is informed, and the Marshal is pleased, and a note goes into a Warden ledger about a captain who reports things. Kettle is on the wagon at dawn regardless, and does not look at you for two days. The rest of the company noticed which way you jumped, and has filed it.

choices.label: Gather the company.

nodes.body: The last hour in Gallowmere: the company assembled in the yard with its kit checked twice, the moor going blue-black beyond the stockade, and the rain easing into something merely unpleasant. Everything has been settled except the shape of your leaving, and that has to be settled tonight.

choices.label: March at first light, light kit, good order.
March tonight in the rain, ahead of the Rooks.
Spend the advance properly before you move.
Sell the commission on and be a live coward.

nodes.body: Out at first light with the bell, light kit and good order, and the stockade gate closing behind the last man in the company. The moor opens ahead of you like a held breath, and for the first mile it is almost possible to enjoy the walk.

choices.label: Take the causeway.

nodes.body: A night march in horizontal rain to steal a day on the Rooks: four miles of it, in the dark, on a track nobody can see. By the time the sky greys the company is wet through to the skin, and the head start has been paid for in the only currency the moor accepts.

choices.label: Take the causeway.

nodes.body: The advance sits on the table and there is exactly one morning available in which to spend it. Nyre wants a mule, salt, oil and eighty feet of rope; Dellach wants moor-iron and a warded haft for the poleaxe. One of them is purchasing endurance and the other is purchasing edge, and unfortunately both of them are entirely correct.

choices.label: Mule, salt, oil, and rope.
A moor-iron blade and a warded haft.

nodes.body: A bad-tempered mule named Preacher, four stone of salt, a cask of oil and eighty feet of tarred rope. The company jokes about the mule the whole way out of the gate, and will stop joking about the mule well inside the week.

choices.label: Take the causeway.

nodes.body: Moor-iron, bought off a smith who would not meet your eye while he wrapped it: a short heavy blade and a warded haft for Dellach's poleaxe. It is cold in the hand in a way that ordinary iron is not, and worth every coin if even half the stories are true.

choices.label: Take the causeway.

nodes.body: The causeway out of Gallowmere ends at the edge of the Barrow Moor, which is the last dry ground anybody will stand on for two days. Three ways go forward from here. There is the drover track along the dykes, the straight line across open moor that saves a day, and the old dwarf road, which goes under the hill's shoulder and comes out where nobody living can tell you.

choices.label: Take the drover track along the dykes.
Cut straight across the moor and save a day.
Follow the old dwarf road under the hill.

nodes.body: You ride south out of Gallowmere with your pride intact and nothing else whatsoever, and the Rooks' banner goes up over the refused commission before you are clear of the stockade. Dellach says the thing you already know exactly once and then never mentions it again, which is that pride does not winter well.

Out on the moor after dark behind a drunk with a rushlight, following a taproom story to its source. The file of lamps is considerably closer than it appeared from the window, and when it halts, it halts in order to count. The burner runs immediately. The last thing anybody in the company hears is a number, pronounced carefully, in a voice with no throat behind it.

Steel drawn in a Warden town puts the whole company in the stockade cells before midnight. The commission is struck at dawn and handed to the Rooks in the yard, and Redd's clerk reads the forfeiture out loud through the bars in a level voice while Corrow waits outside, being careful not to smile.

Forty crowns, split five ways in a wet yard, and the Rooks ride out with your paper before noon. The company is alive and paid and finished as a company, because the story that gets told in every taproom between here and the Ledger cities is the one where the Ninth Sword sold.

Halloway's ink dries on nine years of the company's labour in the time it takes to read the clause twice, which you do not do. The iron is forgotten, the ledger is promised, and Nyre walks out of the counting room without a word, because she has understood what you signed and you have not.

The commission is sold on cheap and the road south is taken before the weather turns for good. The moor keeps its garrison and its iron and its arithmetic. The question of what happened under that hill follows the company down every road it takes afterwards, and it is patient, and it never quite closes.

The drover track runs along the dyke crest with peat water on both sides the colour of strong tea, and somebody has set sheep skulls on posts every hundred paces for reasons that are not agricultural. The hill of Kar Duhn sits on the skyline like a grey knuckle. It does not appear to get any closer for the first two hours of walking.

choices.label: Keep to the dyke crest, single file.
Drop to the drove road below the bank.
Stop at the gibbet cage where the tracks cross.

nodes.body: The crest offers sightlines in every direction and no cover of any description, in a crosswind strong enough to make the whole company walk like drunks. Dellach observes that anything watching this stretch of moor has been watching the Ninth Sword for two solid hours. He does not develop the point, because he does not need to.

choices.label: Press on to the sluice.
Get down out of sight below the bank.

nodes.body: The drove road below the bank is shin-deep and sucking, and it takes the wind off your faces at the price of everything else. The mule fights every single yard of it, Odd goes down twice, and the company buys its shelter with its legs.

choices.label: Climb out at the sluice.

nodes.body: There is a Warden's gibbet where the tracks cross, with a man still in it, tarred and long past complaining about the arrangement. Cut into the post below him is a mark that is not Warden work at all: a ring of nine strokes with the ninth struck through. The chisel work is recent enough that the dust is still sitting in the grooves.

choices.label: Cut the mark out of the post for Ilsabet.
Leave it be; a hanged man is a hanged man.
Camp under it, out of the wind, and move at first light.

nodes.body: The mark comes out of the post in one wedge of oak, and Ilsabet turns it over twice before delivering a careful verdict. It is not a ward and it is not a curse; it is a tally. Somebody has been keeping that tally on Warden property for a considerable time.

choices.label: Pocket it and go on to the sluice.

nodes.body: The dwarf sluice sits at the moor's throat, a channel of cut stone with its gate broken half open, and the black water shooting through the gap is loud enough that the company has to talk over it. Forty feet of the track on the far side has drowned entirely. Whatever crosses here now, crosses wet.

choices.label: Rope a line and wade it.
Go round by the reed island and lose an hour.
Have Ilsabet freeze the gap shut long enough to cross.
Cross dry along the gate's iron beam.

nodes.body: Chest-deep in water cold enough to stop a heart, with the rope line humming and Dellach's shoulders taking the strain on the far bank. Kettle counts everyone through the gap by name, twice, and the second count is the one that matters to her.

choices.label: Keep the line taut and go one at a time.
Let the line go and swim the last of it.

nodes.body: An hour is lost going round by the reed island, and the company arrives dry to the knee and no higher, which is a bargain. From the island's high point you get the first clear view of the barrow gate, a mile off: nine lamp hooks on the arch, and every one of them occupied.

choices.label: Rejoin the track and make camp.

nodes.body: Salt and glass and Ilsabet's flat working voice, and the gap crusts over in grey lace that holds for something under two minutes. The company crosses entirely dry. On the far bank she sits down harder than she means to, and will not be helped up by anybody.

choices.label: Give her a minute, then make camp.

nodes.body: The open moor is pale tussock and black pool, with no track across it and no horizon that stays where you last put it, which is the particular kind of country that remains flat until the moment it kills you. The hill is somewhere ahead. Between here and it lies a full day of educated guesswork.

choices.label: Keep to the tussock lines and go slow.
Push hard and straight and save the daylight.
Follow the fresh path somebody else cut through it.

nodes.body: The slow way has Kettle reading the tussocks like a page and calling each step aloud, with the company strung out behind her in single file and nobody complaining. Four miles are bought with six hours of daylight, and not one person gets wet above the knee.

choices.label: Cut peat for the fire at the old workings.

nodes.body: The fast way works admirably until Sten goes in to the chest, and the moor takes his spear and one boot as payment for the lesson. The company spends its entire saved hour hauling him out by the belt, and afterwards nobody suggests that the hour was ever real.

choices.label: Slow down; the moor made its point.
Keep the pace and let the moor try again.

nodes.body: Something has cut a path through the tussocks, days old and as wide as a wagon, except that no wagon made it. Something was dragged this way in quantity, repeatedly, and the drag marks have small hard footprints on both sides of them going in one direction only.

choices.label: Follow it and see what was dragged.
Get off it and back to open moor.
Set an ambush on the path and wait.

nodes.body: The butchering ground at the path's end has been organised by somebody methodical: Warden kit stacked by type, boots in one pile and belts in another, the relief patrol's shields with the paint carefully scraped off. There is very little blood anywhere. The tidiness of the arrangement is considerably worse than the smell.

choices.label: Take the Warden signet and the dispatch case.
Bury what can be buried and let Nyre say the words.
Back away now; the Fenkin are still close.
Follow the small footprints home.

nodes.body: A Warden signet and a leather dispatch case come off the top of the pile, and the case is still sealed, which is the interesting part. The seal is not a Warden seal. Nyre recognises the factor's stamp on it immediately, and her face closes like a shut account.

choices.label: Get off the path and go to ground.

nodes.body: An hour of hard work in wet peat, and Nyre says the burial words properly over eleven Wardens while the company stands sweating and silent. Dellach keeps watch throughout, facing the direction the small footprints go. It costs you the last of the light and buys something that cannot be spent.

choices.label: Move before the light goes entirely.

nodes.body: Two hours flat in cold water, and then eleven minutes of violence that goes almost exactly as planned. Four Fenkin scouts lie dead along the path, and one of them is wearing a Warden's boots and a ring of nine strokes cut into bone on a thong at his throat.

choices.label: Take the tally-ring and get off the path.

nodes.body: The old peat workings have a cut face standing higher than a man, and in it, preserved down to the eyelashes, is a bog body. The hands are bound at the wrist. A strip of iron has been laid in the open mouth, deliberately, and the peat above the body has not been disturbed for a century.

choices.label: Have Ilsabet read the iron in the mouth.
Take the iron and go.
Cover the face and leave the man his iron.

nodes.body: Ilsabet reads the strip by lamplight with her nose an inch above the metal, and pronounces it dwarf-cut, a pay-tally, one of an original nine. The final word takes her longest to render into common speech, and when she has it she looks genuinely unhappy. It is not a number at all but a rank: the ninth hand, the one that keeps the count for the other eight.

choices.label: Make camp while there is light to choose ground.

nodes.body: The dwarf road runs under the hill's shoulder in a cut so straight it insults the moor on either side of it, roofed in places with slabs the size of doors. Every ninth pace there is a lamp niche cut into the wall at shoulder height. Several of the niches have been swept out recently by somebody with a brush.

choices.label: Walk the open cut where the sky still shows.
Take the covered gallery where the roof stands.
Back out and rejoin the dyke track at the sluice.

nodes.body: In the open cut, where the sky still shows overhead, a legion milestone stands at the bend with nine notches cut beneath the imperial hand. Beside it a niche holds a clay lamp, and there is oil in the lamp, and the oil has not been standing long enough to gum.

choices.label: Take the oil; a full lamp is a full lamp.
Leave the niche exactly as you found it.
Duck into the covered gallery instead.

nodes.body: The lamp is decanted into your own reservoir, and it is good clean oil, better than anything bought in Gallowmere. Kettle points out the thing you had already arrived at yourself: somebody fills these niches on a schedule, and that somebody is going to notice the level.

choices.label: Push on to the camp ground.

nodes.body: The covered gallery is dry and dark and echoes wrong, with the roof slabs holding everywhere except the far end, where a fall has closed the way entirely. While the company stands looking at it, something in the rubble of the fall shifts once, with the sound of a chair being moved in another room.

choices.label: Dig through the fall.
Take the crawl on the left of it.
Back out and take the open cut's lamp niche instead.

nodes.body: An hour of moving stone by hand in the dark, with Dellach and Odd at the face and dust in every throat, until the fall gives up a gap you could get a shoulder through. A draught comes out of the gap immediately, and it smells of lamp oil and old meat in roughly equal measure.

choices.label: Take the gap while the fall is quiet.
Widen it properly first; do it once, do it right.

nodes.body: Sixty feet of crawling on your elbows with the roof riding your back, and then the space opens out into a chamber. Nine lamp niches, every one burnt dry, and nine hooks above them. Underneath the hooks a body is sitting in a good southern coat with a Ledger seal still pinned to the breast and its hands folded neatly in its lap.

choices.label: Take the Ledger seal off the body.
Back out; nine dead lamps is a message and you have read it.

nodes.body: Factor Halloway's own seal comes away in your hand, still bright. The dead man's satchel holds a fair copy of the Kar Duhn pay account, and somebody has circled the ninth signature on it twice in a southern ink that has not run despite everything.

choices.label: Take it and get out into air.

nodes.body: The last camp is a dry hummock within sight of the barrow gate a mile off, and from here you can see nine lamps burning on nine hooks in broad daylight for nobody's benefit whatsoever. The company's mood has arrived at the specific quiet of people doing arithmetic they do not like.

choices.label: Full watch, no fire, no talking.
Fire, hot food, and a short watch; they need it.
Send Kettle forward to look at the gate.
Break camp and arrive before dawn.
Call it. The moor has beaten better companies.

nodes.body: A cold camp and a full watch, and at the third hour a file of lamps comes along the dwarf road below the hummock. Nine of them, entirely unhurried. At the head of the file somebody is counting aloud in a language that appears to have considerably more numbers in it than are strictly necessary.

choices.label: Let it pass and log the hour.
Follow it at distance.
Leave Bram on watch and get an hour's sleep.

nodes.body: One small fire in a peat pit, hot food, dry socks, and ninety minutes of genuine sleep each, which the company has needed for two days. At the end of it there is something standing at the very edge of the firelight that does not come closer and does not leave.

choices.label: Stand to and challenge it.
Douse everything and lie flat until it goes.

nodes.body: The challenge is given in the Warden's form, three times, as the drill requires. On the third asking the shape at the fire's edge answers with a number instead of a name, and then it waits, patiently, to see whether anybody in the Ninth Sword knows what is supposed to be said next.

choices.label: Say nothing more; hold the line and let it go.
Answer it. Give it the next number.

nodes.body: Kettle returns at dusk with a scout's report and a distinctly bad colour in her face. The gate stands open a hand's width, the nine lamps have been trimmed and tended recently, and a Warden's shield has been nailed to the post as a public notice. In the mud in front of the arch there are boot prints going in, and none whatsoever coming back out.

choices.label: Go in openly at the gate in the morning.
Wait for the next file and go in behind it.
Send her in alone to open the way for the rest.

nodes.body: The file goes up the causeway at the third hour, and the company follows it in at forty paces, moving on the lamp-count and learning the rhythm of the thing as it goes. You arrive at the gate with the door still swinging gently from whatever went through it ahead of you.

choices.label: Go in.

nodes.body: Following nine lamps across a black moor at forty paces means staying close enough to hear the count, and close enough to hear one man in the file who is plainly not walking under his own management. After a quarter hour Ilsabet says the thing everybody has independently noticed. The count is not going upward. It is going round.

choices.label: Keep silent and follow to the gate.
Take the count up with them and walk in as one of nine.

nodes.body: The company falls into the file and takes up the count, with Kettle's voice steady on numbers she learned when she was eleven years old. Eleven minutes of walking in that rhythm is enough for anybody. By the end of it you understand precisely what the file is for, and what it is carrying, and to whom.

choices.label: Break off at the gate before the count comes round.

nodes.body: Camp is struck at midnight and the last mile is walked in the dark for no better reason than the captain's impatience with waiting. The company arrives at the barrow gate grey-faced and short-tempered, with the eastern sky only just going pale behind them.

choices.label: Look at what you came for.

nodes.body: The barrow gate of Kar Duhn is a dwarf-cut arch driven into the hillside, and its lintel carries a carving of a door held shut by nine irons. A Warden's shield has been nailed to the post with the paint scraped off it, and nine lamps burn on nine hooks in broad daylight. The great door itself stands open the width of a hand and no wider, exactly as the last dispatch described it.

choices.label: Go in by the open door.
Send Kettle up the spoil chute and follow.
Have Ilsabet break the mason's postern.
Sit on the gate and watch it for a full day first.

nodes.body: A day spent watching a door teaches the company precisely one thing. At the ninth hour, two men in Warden cloaks that do not fit them come out through the gap, take down three of the lamps, and carry them back inside. Neither man uses his hands to open the door, and neither of them so much as glances at the moor.

choices.label: Enough watching. Go in by the door.
Go up the spoil chute where nobody counts.
Take the mason's postern.

nodes.body: It is a good dry camp in the lee of the gibbet post, genuinely out of the wind for the first time in two days of walking. At the third hour the lamps arrive along the track and stop, and a voice begins a count. It includes the sleepers by name, in the order in which they lay down, and the ninth name on the list is the captain's own.

The iron beam is wet, and the crosswind arrives in the middle of the third crossing rather than the first. The sluice takes two of the company through the gap in less time than it takes to shout a warning, and afterwards the water goes on being exactly as loud as it was before.

The rope goes in cold that stops thought before it stops the hands, and the current under the sluice turns out to be considerably deeper than it looked and to be going somewhere the dwarves cut on purpose. The moor keeps what it takes and does not make any fuss about it.

The pace is kept and the moor's second attempt succeeds where its first only made a point. A false floor of root and water puts three of the company in past the shoulder, the mule goes down and stays down, and Kar Duhn remains a grey knuckle on a horizon that nobody from the Ninth Sword ever reaches.

The small footprints are followed home to a fen camp of roughly two hundred, which is about a hundred and ninety more than the plan accounted for. The company is taken alive, because alive is specifically what this camp is paid to deliver. A Fenkin quartermaster enters five additional marks in a tally he keeps on behalf of somebody living under the hill.

The fall is widened properly, because Dellach is right that it should be done once and done correctly. The roof above it has been holding for a century with considerable patience, and it chooses this hour to stop. Forty feet of dwarf gallery comes down in the time it takes a man to look up.

The next number is given aloud, and the thing at the edge of the firelight accepts it as a valid answer and steps into the light to complete the transaction. Whatever the Ninth Sword becomes after that is counted, and kept, and is no longer in any useful sense a company.

Kettle goes in alone at the second hour, and the gate closes to a thumb's width behind her within a minute of her passing through it. After four hours of nothing whatsoever, the company withdraws across the moor without the only person who knew the way down. That ends the contract, and something else besides.

An hour's sleep, and fen-runner arithmetic. The watch is abandoned somewhere around the second hour, and the mule goes south with what remains of the advance and all of the spare lamp oil. The company wakes in a cold camp within sight of a job it can no longer afford to attempt.

The sensible decision is made a mile short of the gate, and the report is written honestly, and the fee is returned in full. It is the correct call. You will spend the next nine years hearing the Rooks tell it differently in every taproom between here and the Ledger cities.

The last quarter mile of causeway runs to the barrow gate entirely in the open, with the arch ahead and the Warden's shield on its post catching whatever light remains. Nine lamps hang on nine hooks, freshly trimmed. In the mud in front of the arch, unmistakably, there are boot prints going in and none of them coming back out again.

choices.label: Walk up the causeway in good order.
Come at it off the path, over the spoil heap.
Send the mule up the causeway first and watch what happens.

nodes.body: The mule is sent up the causeway alone as an experiment. Preacher walks to the gate, stops, stands there for nine full seconds, and then goes in through a gap he cannot possibly fit through. The company stands in the mud afterwards without its salt, its oil, or any remaining appetite for the arch.

From a foot away the great door is dwarf bronze laid over iron, standing open exactly a hand's width, and the air coming out of the gap is warm and smells of lamp oil and wet stone. The edge of the gap has been worn smooth at shoulder height by traffic, which is not something a door does to itself.

choices.label: Go through the gap one at a time.
Lever the door wider with the poleaxe haft.
Take the Warden's shield off the post first.
Knock, and see who keeps the door.

nodes.body: You go through sideways, one at a time, with packs passed through afterwards, and Dellach manages it last and worst of anybody. While Odd is still in the gap the door moves a finger's width inward, unhurriedly, on no draught whatsoever, and then stops again as though it had merely been thinking.

choices.label: Get everyone through fast and form up inside.
Hold the door with the haft while the last man squeezes.

nodes.body: The poleaxe haft goes into the gap with Dellach's entire weight behind it, and the door comes open two feet with a groan that travels down into the hill and keeps travelling for longer than seems reasonable. There is a pause afterwards. Then something a long way below begins to count.

choices.label: Go in fast, before it finishes counting.
Take the Warden's shield off the post before you go in.

nodes.body: The Warden's shield comes off the post in two blows and turns over heavily in your hands. On the inside face, somebody with plenty of time and no light at all has scratched three lines with the tongue of a belt buckle. Eight hold, nine counts, do not answer it when it uses your name, and the lettering deteriorates badly toward the end.

choices.label: Take the shield and go in by the gap.

nodes.body: The spoil chute lies on the hill's flank, a throat of loose scree dropping forty feet into complete darkness, cut by dwarves who wanted somewhere to throw waste. The stones at the lip have been polished by something coming up and down it since. Nothing has thrown waste out of here for nine hundred years.

choices.label: Rope down in order, quietly.
Send Kettle down first and follow her signal.
Slide it. It is only scree.

nodes.body: Forty feet of rope work in the dark gets everybody down to the bottom with skinned palms and nothing worse than that. The mule stays tethered above, expressing his opinion of the arrangement at considerable and sustained volume for as long as anybody can still hear him. Cold water is waiting at the foot of the chute, and it is deeper than the lamplight suggested.

choices.label: Wade out of the sump.

nodes.body: Kettle goes down first on a single line with two whistles agreed for clear, which is the arrangement she always insists on. The whistles do not come. There is nothing at all for six minutes, which is four minutes longer than the arrangement allows for, and then one whistle, very quietly.

choices.label: Go down on her signal when it finally comes.
Go down now, fast, and find her.
Wait the full ten minutes as agreed.

nodes.body: The sump at the chute's foot is a tank of cut stone holding waist-deep black water, with an iron grate at the far end admitting to the vault proper. A quantity of material has collected against the grate over the past several months. Most of it is cloth, and most of the cloth is unmistakably Warden issue.

choices.label: Force the grate and go through into the hall.
Follow the sump wall to the dry gallery.
Take what is caught in the grate.
Dive the outflow and see where it goes.

nodes.body: What the grate has kept: a Warden's tally-iron on a thong, a sodden dispatch bag with the writing gone, and a boot with the foot still laced into it. Nyre takes charge of the boot before anybody can make a joke about it, which is probably why nobody does.

choices.label: Force the grate and go on into the hall.

nodes.body: The dry gallery is unlit, and it smells like a larder because that is what it is. Eleven bodies have been stacked with genuine care in a side bay, and four pale drinkers sleep among them, long-limbed and ribbed like greyhounds, their hands folded neatly in front of them like men at prayer.

choices.label: Withdraw along the wall to the hall.
Burn the bay with the lamp oil.
Go through quietly and leave them fed.
Wake them and fight in the dark, on your terms.

nodes.body: Oil, flint, and a side bay that goes up like a hayrick. Three drinkers die in the fire without ever properly waking, and the fourth goes away down the gallery screaming in a register that hurts the teeth. The smoke follows the company for an hour and announces its position for two.

choices.label: Move on into the hall before the fourth brings company.

nodes.body: Eleven minutes of moving past sleeping drinkers at the pace of a minute hand, with Ilsabet laying a salt line behind each footfall. The fourth one opens its eyes as the last of you goes by, considers the situation without moving at all, and then visibly decides not to bother.

choices.label: Keep going and do not look back.
Take a hoard-tooth from the bay on the way out.

nodes.body: The mason's postern sits round the hill's shoulder: a dwarf door about the size of a coffin lid, sealed with lead and inscribed with mason's marks. Beside it, cut into the living rock, is a tally of nine strokes, and the dust from the ninth stroke has not yet been washed out by rain.

choices.label: Let Ilsabet unpick the seal properly; it will take an hour.
Break it with the poleaxe and go in loud.
Read the tally beside it first.

nodes.body: Read closely, the tally is nine strokes with the ninth struck through, and below it a second hand has kept a running count in the hundreds, grouped in nines. The lower groups go back further than the lead in the door has been cold. Ilsabet stops translating before she reaches the bottom.

choices.label: Have Ilsabet open the seal properly.
Break it; whoever keeps that count already knows.

nodes.body: An hour of quiet work: lead cut away in curls, mason's marks answered one at a time in Ilsabet's chalk, and the door finally opening inward on cold air. The corridor beyond has dust on the floor that nothing with hands has walked through for a very long time.

choices.label: Go in.

nodes.body: The postern breaks in four blows, which the hill repeats back to you for considerably longer than four blows deserve. Then a lamp appears at the far end of the corridor, coming up at walking pace, held by somebody who does not hurry, does not call out, and does not appear to be armed.

choices.label: Take him alive.
Put him down quietly and move.
Challenge whoever is behind that lamp.

nodes.body: The weighing floor of Kar Duhn is a hall of standing scales, with nine iron-bound chests ranged along one wall and every one of them open and empty. The floor is a mosaic showing a door held shut by nine hands. Three ways lead on: the barracks arch, the counting-room passage, and a gallery from which the smell of fresh lamp oil is unmistakable.

choices.label: Clear the barracks arch first.
Go to the counting room; that is the contract.
Follow the smell of fresh oil.
Read the mosaic on the floor properly.

nodes.body: Under the dust the mosaic resolves into something specific: eight hands laid flat against a door of nine irons, and a ninth hand standing apart in front of it holding a tally-board. A border of dwarf letters runs the whole way round the design, worn shallow by nine centuries of boots.

choices.label: Have Ilsabet read the border.
Enough floor-reading; the counting room is the contract.

nodes.body: Ilsabet reads the border aloud in careful dwarf, and it becomes clear within a line and a half that this is not a dedication. The door is not a lock but a lid: eight hands to hold it down, and one hand to keep the count and to bring what is owed on the appointed day. The final clause of the border is a price, payable in nines, in perpetuity.

choices.label: Take that to the counting room.

nodes.body: The garrison barracks holds forty bunks made up to inspection standard, kit stowed, boots paired at the foot of each bed. The far third of the room has been walled off from floor to ceiling with a barricade of shields and bunk timber. The barricade was built from this side, by people who then stayed on this side.

choices.label: Take the shield wall apart.
Search the sergeant's chest.
Sleep here in shifts; the company is spent.
Strip the kit and coin and go home rich.

nodes.body: Opened just enough to see through, the barricade gives up its contents. Eleven Wardens are seated shoulder to shoulder along the wall behind it, drained to paper, hands folded, boots off and paired neatly beside each of them. The fourth man from the left is slowly turning his head toward the gap.

choices.label: Put it down properly and quickly.
Ask it a question.
Wall it back up and walk away.
Cut it free and carry it out for the Marshal to see.

nodes.body: One clean stroke from Dellach, and afterwards Nyre sets the man's boots straight and writes his name in her book from the tag at his collar. She says the words at half volume because there is not time for the whole rite, and she notes that fact down as well.

choices.label: Go through the sergeant's chest.

nodes.body: The question is asked, and it is answered in numbers, patiently, in the manner of a clerk responding to a query about an account. Eight, it says, and then a pause of exactly the right length, and then eight again. When Nyre asks who the ninth is, the head turns further round on its neck and looks directly at the company for the first time.

choices.label: Stop there. Put it down and close the wall.
Ask it the ninth question.

nodes.body: The sergeant's chest is unlocked, because there was eventually nothing left worth locking. Inside: a duty roster with nine names struck out in identical ink, an unmarked Warden key-iron blank, and a bottle of paymaster's brandy with two fingers gone out of the neck.

choices.label: Take the roster.
Take the blank iron.
Share the brandy out; they have earned two fingers each.

nodes.body: The roster reads badly on the walk: nine names struck out on nine consecutive days, the last of them the paymaster's own. Against every struck name somebody has written a single word in the margin, and Ilsabet says the word is the dwarf term used in accounts for tendered.

choices.label: Take the counting-room passage.

nodes.body: An unmarked key-iron, the same length and gauge as the ones the door is carved with, entirely blank where the tally should be cut. Ilsabet takes it off you, wraps it in salt-cloth, and puts it in her own pack without offering any explanation for why she is smiling.

choices.label: Take the counting-room passage.

nodes.body: Two fingers of paymaster's brandy each, which is not much and turns out to be exactly enough. The company stands in a dead man's barracks drinking a dead man's drink, and everybody's hands come back to them within about ten minutes, which is worth more than the brandy cost anybody.

choices.label: Take the counting-room passage.

nodes.body: Four hours of shifts on made beds in a barracks that smells strongly of other men's boots. Nobody sleeps well and everybody sleeps, and at the end of it the company is capable of having the day it is about to have, which was not true before.

choices.label: Take the counting-room passage.

nodes.body: The counting room holds a table forty feet long with nine balances set out in a row along it, and the winter pay-ledger lies open at its final page beneath a lamp that is still burning. In the lock of the ninth chest a key-iron stands where a hand let go of it and did not come back.

choices.label: Read the last page before you touch anything.
Take the pay-ledger; the Marshal wants the ledger.
Take the ninth iron out of the lock.
Search the clerk's alcove behind the table.
Load the remaining plate and withdraw with salvage.

nodes.body: The last page shows a winter's pay entered in full and balanced against nothing at all, with nine names tendered in a clerk's failing hand. At the foot of the column, in a different pen and pressed hard enough to tear the paper, somebody has written four words. We are the payment.

choices.label: Take the iron out of the lock and get out.
Leave it all where it lies and search the alcove.

nodes.body: The pay-ledger comes off the table into Nyre's satchel: four pounds of paper and the entire second half of your contract. As it lifts clear the lamp above it gutters and goes out, as though the room had only been keeping the thing lit until somebody arrived to read it.

choices.label: Take the iron from the lock as well.
Leave the iron; the ledger is what was asked for.

nodes.body: The ninth key-iron draws out of the lock as cold as the inside of a well and considerably heavier than its size argues for. The instant it clears the wards every lamp in the upper vault dips at once, together. Far below, something that had been counting steadily all day starts again from one.

choices.label: Wrap it in Ilsabet's salt-cloth before you carry it.
Put it straight back in the lock and take only paper.
Pocket it and search the clerk's alcove.
Carry it in your mouth, the way the bog man carried his.

nodes.body: Salt-cloth, then oilcloth, then the middle of the pack, and the difference is immediate: the pressure behind everybody's eyes simply stops. Ilsabet says the thing nobody wanted said out loud, which is that the pressure was not the iron. It was being noticed through the iron.

choices.label: Make for the stair by way of the schedule board.

nodes.body: The iron goes back into the lock exactly as it was found, to the quarter turn. The lamps steady, the count somewhere below stops in the middle of a number, and the company stands in a room that has just declined, quite politely, to keep any of them.

choices.label: Search the clerk's alcove and get out.

nodes.body: Behind the table is the clerk's alcove: a cot that has been slept in for months, a private tally scratched into the plaster in groups of nine, a jar of clean water. At floor level somebody has broken a hole through the wall, and warm air is coming up out of it.

choices.label: Read the clerk's private tally.
Put a lamp down the hole and look.
Leave it; read the schedule board and take the stair.
Go down the hole now, while it is quiet.

nodes.body: The clerk's plaster tally is not a record of days at all, it is a record of deliveries, kept in groups of nine for eleven years by somebody with a steady and unhurried hand. In the final group there are only eight strokes cut into the plaster. Where the ninth stroke should be, he has written a single word in common speech, and the word is mine.

choices.label: Go on to the schedule board.

nodes.body: A lamp lowered on a bootlace shows eleven feet of broken wall and then a floor. On the floor there is a set of small neat footprints in the dust, and they go round in a circle, and they have gone round that same circle several hundred times without ever leaving it.

choices.label: Pull the lamp up and go by the schedule board.
Reach down and take up what is lying by the footprints.

nodes.body: The lamp gallery holds nine niches in a row with all nine lamps trimmed and full, and an oil store stacked to the roof behind them. A schedule board hangs on the wall in chalk, listing hours in a hand that takes its work seriously. On a bench beneath the board a lamp-keeper is asleep with a tally-book rising and falling on his chest.

choices.label: Take him alive and ask him everything.
Wake him politely and talk terms.
Kill him and take the book.
Read the board and leave him sleeping.
Put a light in the oil store on your way past.

nodes.body: He is taken with a hand across his mouth and offers no resistance of any kind whatsoever. He is nineteen years old and a Warden's son by the belt he is wearing, and he is so thoroughly relieved to have been caught by people who ask questions that he starts answering before anybody has managed to put one to him. Nyre gets him a blanket before the interrogation begins.

choices.label: Let him talk it all the way out.
Ask only what you need: the safe way down.
Promise to take him out with you when you go.

nodes.body: It comes out in a flat exhausted voice, the whole of it, with no prompting required after the first minute. The Compact is a contract, and the thing behind the Ninefold Door is neither dead nor intended ever to be dead. Eight irons hold the lid down, the ninth hand keeps the count and delivers what is owed, and the garrison, in the end, was simply what happened to be owed.

choices.label: Read the schedule board with new eyes.

nodes.body: He gives you the route and nothing else at all, gratefully. The great stair lies behind the ninth niche. There are two landings where nobody should stop for any reason whatsoever, and there is one hour of the day when the stair is in use by somebody else and must be left entirely alone.

choices.label: Read the schedule board.

nodes.body: The promise is made out loud in front of witnesses, and Nyre writes it in her book, and the boy's whole posture changes as she does it. He gives you the route, the hours, the count, and a warning about the ninth hour delivered in the manner of a man confessing to a murder.

choices.label: Read the schedule board together.

nodes.body: Woken civilly and offered a chair he is already sitting in, the keeper turns out to be a negotiator rather than a victim. He will give you the stair and the hours in exchange for one thing: the company carries a parcel out for him, unopened, and leaves it at a Ledger house.

choices.label: Accept his terms and take the stair.
Break faith; bind him and ask properly.
Take his other offer: one hour in the file, and safe passage.

nodes.body: The tally-book comes off a boy who never woke up. Nyre's face closes like a ledger at year end, Kettle finds something to look at on the far wall, and below in the hill the count falters on a number, holds for a moment, and then deliberately starts again from one.

choices.label: Take the book and move before the count comes up.
Put on his cloak and carry his lamp.

nodes.body: A keeper's cloak that does not fit anybody in the company, and a keeper's lamp held at a keeper's height. It is an adequate disguise against anything that counts by lamp-height, and no disguise at all against anything that counts by weight, and nobody says the second part out loud.

choices.label: Read the schedule board.

nodes.body: The schedule board is chalk on slate, and it is entirely legible: nine niches, nine hours, the lamps to be trimmed on the hour without exception. The ninth hour has been ringed twice, and beside the ring the keeper has written four words in an extremely careful hand, which are do not be on the stair. Behind the ninth niche, the great stair goes down.

choices.label: Go down now, well clear of the ninth hour.
Wait for the ninth hour and go down behind the file.
Douse all nine lamps before you go down.

nodes.body: Four hours of waiting in the oil store, and then the ninth hour arrives exactly on schedule. Nine lamps are lifted off nine hooks by hands that nobody in the company looks at directly, a count starts down the stair, and the Ninth Sword steps into the forty paces of silence behind it.

choices.label: Take the stair.

nodes.body: Nine lamps are pinched out one after another, and the quality of the silence changes with every one of them. After the ninth, the hill is not quiet at all. It is attentive, in the way a room becomes attentive when everybody in it has stopped pretending to read.

choices.label: Take the stair immediately, in the dark.
Wait to see what comes up to relight them.

nodes.body: The great stair of Kar Duhn lies behind the ninth niche, nine feet wide and cut by dwarves who expected regular traffic on it, dropping away in long flights into air that is warm and moving and ought to be neither. Somewhere far below it there is water. Above the water there is a smell like a forge that was left to go out very slowly.

choices.label: Go down in order with lamps lit.
Go down dark, one hand on the wall.
Rope the stair and send Kettle a flight ahead.
Turn around. Take what you have and get out.

nodes.body: Three knocks on dwarf bronze, and the door opens the rest of the way from the inside without anything visible touching it. A voice out of the dark invites the Ninth Sword in by the correct number, which is five, and none of the five is ever afterwards able to explain to anybody why they went.

The haft holds the door for eleven seconds and then folds along its length, and the door closes back to its hand's width with a man still in the gap. The company ends up on both sides of a foot of bronze that will not move again for any lever anybody has left.

The chute is taken the fast way, and the scree comes with you all at once, which is what scree does. The company arrives in the sump under four tons of moving stone in complete darkness, and that is not a fight, or an ambush, or in any way survivable.

The full ten minutes are kept exactly as agreed. Then the rope comes up with its end cut clean, no scout on it and no signal following it, and the company stands on a hillside at dusk with no way down that anybody trusts and a long walk to Gallowmere to explain the fact.

The outflow is dived on one breath: eleven feet of cut stone, then a turn the wrong way, then the discovery that dwarves built their drains to be cleaned from the far end and never once from this one. The turn is too tight to reverse in.

Four pale drinkers are woken deliberately in a dark gallery by a company that had a plan and had rehearsed the plan twice. It survives contact for about eleven seconds, which is until the second one comes off the ceiling behind the line rather than in front of it. Afterwards the gallery is simply a larder with rather more in it than it had before.

A hoard-tooth is lifted from the bay on the way past, which takes two seconds. The fourth drinker decides, on reflection, that it is worth bothering after all, and the salt line behind the company's feet turns out to have been laid for people who keep walking forward.

A challenge is shouted down a dwarf corridor, and the answer comes back correctly in the Warden form, word for word, in the voice of the man whose shield is nailed to the gate post outside. The lamp keeps coming at walking pace, and nobody in the company manages to move.

Forty sets of Warden kit and a garrison's small coin go out by mule and sell in Gallowmere for genuinely good money inside a week. The commission is unfulfilled, and the pay-ledger is still lying open on its table under a lamp that nobody will trim again. The receipt in the Marshal's file records precisely what kind of company the Ninth Sword turned out to be.

A drained Warden is cut out of the barricade and carried toward daylight on a shield, on the sound principle that evidence wins arguments with Wardens. The thing on the shield waits until the second landing before demonstrating what it was so carefully kept alive in order to do.

The ninth question is asked aloud, and it is answered without hesitation. The answer is the company's own names, given back in the order they came through the door, together with the approximate hour of each arrival. Along the wall all eleven Wardens fold their hands in the same manner at the same moment, and then look up together.

The remaining plate is loaded and walked out by the postern, declared honestly as salvage, and taxed at the proper rate. Redd reads the declaration without any expression at all before asking the only question that matters to him, which is where his pay-ledger has got to.

The ninth iron is carried in the mouth, the way the bound man in the peat was carrying his, because both hands are needed on the rope. There is not time, afterwards, to spit it out and explain that the arrangement was purely practical, and the iron does not accept the distinction.

ending.title: As the Bog Man Carried His

nodes.body: Eleven feet down a broken wall into a room where the footprints go round and round in a circle without ever leaving it. The circle turns out, on closer inspection with a lamp held low, to have a middle. The middle is occupied, and it has been occupied for eleven years, and it has been waiting for precisely this arrangement to present itself.

An arm goes through the hole in the wall to take up what is lying there, which is a lamp, and the lamp is still warm. A hand closes on the wrist out of the dark with the unhurried grip of something that has done this before and knows exactly how long it takes.

ending.title: What Was Lying by the Footprints

nodes.body: A light is put into an oil store holding a year's supply, and the gallery becomes a flue. The fire goes down the great stair ahead of the company, because that is where the air was going, and at the bottom of the stair it finds something that does not object to fire in the slightest.

One hour in the file is agreed in exchange for safe passage down, and lamps are issued to everybody, and the count is taken up at the correct number. The hour ends precisely on schedule, exactly as the keeper promised it would. The company is not released, because the file's arithmetic contains no provision of any kind for anybody leaving it.

Nine lamps out, and the company waits in the dark to see who tends them. The answer comes up the stair without a light of its own, relights all nine from the bottom hook upward in the correct order, and takes the trimming of the wicks extremely seriously indeed.

ending.title: What Comes Up to Relight Them

nodes.body: The stair is declined out loud, in front of witnesses, and the upper vault is walked back out through the gap in the great door with the sun coming up behind the moor. The ledger is delivered and the ninth iron is declared and taxed. The written report states plainly that the Ninth Sword did not go down, and Redd files it, and reads it twice.

Four hundred steps with lamps lit, and two landings on the way down. The wall carvings begin as proper mason's work and degrade, somewhere below the first landing, into gouges cut in a hurry by hands that were not dwarf hands and were not holding dwarf tools. On the second landing there is a shrine with nine niches cut into it at eye height.

choices.label: Stop at the shrine and read it.
Straight down past both landings.
Take twenty minutes on the first landing; they need it.

nodes.body: Four hundred steps in complete darkness with one hand on the wall, feeling the carvings change under the palm from proper tool-work into something scratched in a hurry. At the ninetieth step something comes up past the company on the outer edge of the stair, entirely unhurried, breathing on a count of nine. It does not touch anybody, and it does not stop counting, and it does not come back.

choices.label: Press flat to the wall and let it pass.
Strike a light; blind is worse than seen.
Count the steps aloud to keep the company together.
Take hold of it as it goes by.

nodes.body: The stair is roped and Kettle goes a full flight ahead of everybody, working on tugs: one for clear, two for wait where you are, three for come down after me. She gives one, and then another, and then a third, and then two in quick succession. After that the rope goes slack in your hands without any signal at all, and it stays slack.

choices.label: Go down fast on the last signal she gave.
Overtake the slack and take the lead yourself.
Haul the rope in and see what is on the end of it.

nodes.body: The stair-shrine holds nine niches, eight of them containing dwarf tokens gone black with age, and the ninth standing empty and warm enough to feel from a foot away. The lip of the shrine has been worn into a groove by something that has been set down there and taken back up a great many times.

choices.label: Leave the ninth niche empty and go down.
Set the ninth iron in the empty niche.
Take one of the eight tokens.

nodes.body: The ninth iron goes into the warm niche, which accepts it the way a lock accepts its own key. The entire hill goes quiet for the length of one breath. Then the count starts again somewhere below, slower than before, apparently satisfied, and entirely uninterested in anybody standing on the stair.

choices.label: Go down and see what you have bought.

nodes.body: A lamp struck on the stair catches the thing on the outside of the flight for exactly one second: a Warden's cloak, a Warden's boots, and above the collar nothing that a helmet would ever fit. It continues upward past the company without turning, and its count does not falter.

choices.label: Go down before it comes back for a second look.

nodes.body: The slack rope leads down two flights to Kettle, who is flat against the wall with her own hand over her mouth, alive and extremely angry about it. She points down at the stairfoot, where a work-gang of Fenkin is carrying crates across the bottom of the stair in single file.

choices.label: Wait for the file to pass and go down.

nodes.body: The foot of the great stair is a crossing of ways in warm moving air. To the left a flooded gallery with lamplight lying on the water; ahead the pay-hall doors standing ajar; to the right a chapel light and, below that, the sound of a mill wheel turning. There is a breach in one wall where the vault cut into the old barrow, a cutting-shop with a cold forge beyond it, and at the far end of everything, a door.

choices.label: Take the flooded gallery.
Open the pay-hall doors.
Follow the chapel light.
Go and find the wheel that is turning.
Look into the breach in the wall.
Try the cutting-shop first.
Straight down the hall to the door at the end.
Hail the garrison; somebody down here must be Warden.

nodes.body: The flooded gallery is chest-deep and as warm as bathwater, with lamplight further down it and a flat-bottomed ferry poling toward you. Three Fenkin are aboard, and a crate is lashed amidships. The crate is eighteen inches of dwarf oak, and it is not making crate noises.

choices.label: Swim the gallery past them in the dark water.
Take the ledge above the waterline.
Ambush the ferry from both sides.
Go under and hole the ferry from below.

nodes.body: Sixty yards of warm black water with kit held above the head and the ferry's pole going past close enough to touch. Halfway across, something long turns over in the depth beneath the company, unhurried, indifferent, entirely uninterested in five people making a noise on the surface. It has the manner of an animal that has been extremely well fed for a considerable time.

choices.label: Get out at the far steps and keep going.
Take a breath and see what is under you.

nodes.body: The maintenance ledge above the waterline is eleven inches wide, cut for dwarves without packs rather than men in mail. The ferry passes below close enough that you can hear the crate being spoken to, patiently, in a language that appears to consist entirely of numbers.

choices.label: Work along it to the far end.
Drop on the ferry as it passes underneath.
Take the shortcut where the ledge is broken.

nodes.body: Eleven seconds of violence in waist-deep water puts three Fenkin over the gunwale, and then there is nothing to do except look at the crate. Eighteen inches of dwarf oak, air holes bored through the lid in a ring of nine, and inside it something that has stopped making noise in order to listen to you.

choices.label: Open the crate.
Leave it sealed and take the ferry down the gallery.
Free what is in it, whatever it is.
Take the gang's lamps and pass as the work-file.

nodes.body: The crate holds a Warden of the second relief patrol, alive, wrists bound in a knot Ilsabet recognises and will not name. He is blindfolded, and he is counting under his breath in a rhythm the company has now heard four times today and never once wanted to hear from a human throat.

choices.label: Cut him loose, take him with you, and go.
Ask him what he is counting toward.

nodes.body: The lid comes off and the bound Warden inside is cut free and carried out between two of you, dead weight and still counting steadily. Nyre holds his head as they go and tells him, over and over, that the number is wrong. It is the only argument anybody has available down here, and he does not appear to hear it, but he does not stop being carried either.

choices.label: Carry him and go on to the door.

nodes.body: Three Fenkin lamps held at Fenkin height, and the company poles a ferry down a flooded dwarf gallery in the middle of a work-file that never once looks up. You learn more in that quarter hour than in two days on the moor: what the crates are for, where they go, and how often they go there.

choices.label: Tie up at the door steps and get off the water.

nodes.body: The deep pay-hall is ankle-deep in water and echoes badly. A rack on the far wall holds eight key-irons in eight sockets with a ninth socket standing empty; the pay-bell waits on its stand beside it. The paymaster himself lies face down across his own table, and both his sleeves are empty from the elbow.

choices.label: Turn the paymaster over.
Take the eight irons off the rack.
Read the tally cut into the wall behind the rack.
Ring the pay-bell and see who still answers it.

nodes.body: Turned over, the paymaster has no hands and no other injury anywhere on him. Inside his coat is a confession written in a hand that had to hold the pen in its teeth: that the ninth hand must be a hand that signs, that he signed for nine years, and that in the end he simply stopped.

choices.label: Take the confession and the irons.
Take the confession and go straight to the door.
Look for what happened to his hands.

nodes.body: Up close the rack is warm to the hand, and every one of the eight irons is seated in a socket that is warmer still than the iron. The ninth socket stands empty and worn bright around the mouth, as though something has been drawn out of it and put back a great many times. The whole rack is humming faintly, the way a bowstring hums in the moment before it is loosed.

choices.label: Take one iron and leave the seven seated.
Leave them all exactly where they are.
Take all eight; the Marshal can have the lot.

nodes.body: One iron lifts out, and the rack's hum climbs a full tone as seven irons take up the load of the eighth's absence. Ilsabet says, quietly and with great precision, that the company now has about eleven minutes of the hill's patience remaining, and not one second longer than that.

choices.label: Go to the door.

nodes.body: Behind the rack the wall carries a tally cut in groups of nine, going back nine hundred years in nine distinguishable hands, and then further back in a hand that is not dwarf work at all. In the final group, eight strokes have been cut cleanly and a ninth has been begun.

choices.label: Stop reading and go to the door.
Read it to the end; there is a name at the bottom.

nodes.body: The chapel of the Compact holds nine benches and a wall of tally, and at a clerk's writing desk in front of them a courteous grey man in a good coat stands up as the company comes in. He greets the Ninth Sword by name and by number, apologises for the temperature of the room, and offers the captain the only chair in it. Behind him, the tally-wall runs from floor to ceiling in groups of nine.

choices.label: Hear the offer he means to make.
Ask what the Compact actually pays, and to whom.
Put him down where he stands.
Back out and go and find the wheel instead.
Put a lamp against his tally-wall and burn it.

nodes.body: Coren Vale explains the arithmetic the way a factor explains compound interest. The thing behind the door cannot be killed, and cannot be woken while the count holds. Eight irons hold the lid, the ninth hand keeps the count and delivers what is owed, and the frontier has been paying that instalment for nine hundred years without ever being told.

choices.label: Let him make his offer, then.
Leave him talking and go to the door.

nodes.body: The offer is made plainly and without any threat in it at all. Vale is ninety-one years old and extremely tired, and the ninth hand's place falls vacant on his death. For one of the five, named by the captain today, he will hand over the iron, the ledger, the garrison's entire back pay, and nine more years of the frontier's peace.

choices.label: Refuse, and go for the door.
Counter: the company will settle this another way.
Accept, and name one of them.
Accept, and name yourself.

nodes.body: The counter-offer is put to him straight: the company will close the door properly, all nine irons seated, with no hand at all keeping any count afterwards. Vale's face does something complicated and rather human. In ninety-one years nobody has proposed it to him, and he is not certain that it cannot be done.

choices.label: Go to the door with his blessing, such as it is.

nodes.body: Vale does not defend himself and does not appear to need to, because the chapel undertakes it on his behalf. Nine benches worth of accumulated dust stands up in the approximate shapes of the people who once sat on them. Dellach's first swing passes clean through a grey man's coat and strikes the writing desk standing behind it.

choices.label: Finish him before the benches close.
Break off and run for the door.
Take him hostage and walk him to the door.
Stand and fight the chapel.

nodes.body: Coren Vale dies at his own desk in about the time it takes to say a number aloud, and the count stops. Not slows: stops, everywhere in the hill at once. In the silence afterwards you can hear eight irons taking up a load that they were never designed to carry without a ninth.

choices.label: Run for the door now, while the silence lasts.
Take his tally-book and his ring off the desk.
Wait and see what the count does without a keeper.

nodes.body: Vale's tally-book and the ninth hand's ring come off a dead man's desk together. The book runs to eleven hundred pages of instalments in nine different hands, the last of them his own. The ring is warm, and it is sized, unmistakably, for whichever hand picks it up next.

choices.label: Take both and go to the door.

nodes.body: The wheel-house under the pay-hall holds a dwarf pump the size of a barn, its wheel turning steadily in a race of black water. Three of its nine paddles have been hacked away and a Fenkin crew is working on the fourth with axes, without hurry, in the manner of men on a long contract.

choices.label: Kill the crew and mend the paddles.
Jam the wheel and flood the deep yourselves.
Cross the wheel-race to the door gallery.
Ride the wheel down and see what it drains into.

nodes.body: A short brutal fight in a very loud room, and then an hour of carpentry: Dellach and Odd holding a paddle in place while Ilsabet lashes it. The water in the race drops a hand's width by the end of it, and the deep stays dry a while longer, for whatever that turns out to be worth.

choices.label: Leave it running and go to the door.
Stay and keep it running; somebody has to.

nodes.body: The wheel jams on a poleaxe haft and the race backs up within minutes, sending water the wrong way through nine hundred years of dwarf engineering. It goes down into the lower hall, where the crates are stacked in rows, and where the work-file is still working and has not been warned.

choices.label: Do it and run for the door on the high side.
Do it now, while half the company is still below.

nodes.body: The wheel-race is crossed on the axle housing with the wheel turning a foot behind your head, nine paddles coming round in an order you can learn if you watch for long enough. The gap between two paddles is exactly as wide as one man who does not hesitate in the middle of it.

choices.label: Cross one at a time on the count of the paddles.
Cross together and quickly; the crew has seen you.

nodes.body: The breach in the vault wall opens into the barrow the dwarves cut through and believed they had merely cut through. It is a king's chamber with nine attendants seated around a king who is not present. Their plaques are still perfectly legible, and every one of the nine hands is pointing the same way.

choices.label: Read the attendants' plaques.
Close the breach with rubble and be done with it.
Go through the barrow to the door gallery.
Take the ring off the empty king's chair.

nodes.body: The nine plaques read in order, and they are not names at all but offices: the one who counts, the one who carries, the one who signs, and onward to the ninth, which is the one who is owed. All nine of the stone hands are pointing at the chamber's inner door.

choices.label: Go to the door with that in your head.
Follow where all nine hands are pointing.

nodes.body: Two hours of rubble, mortar dust, and Dellach's shoulder against a slab that does not want to move, and the breach is closed about as well as five people can close it. Everybody understands, without any need to discuss the matter, that this is housekeeping rather than a solution. It will hold for exactly as long as nothing on the other side of it minds being shut in.

choices.label: Go on to the door.

nodes.body: The way through the barrow's inner chamber to the door gallery passes nine empty attendant chairs and one that is occupied. Whatever is sitting in it has been sitting there since before the dwarves cut their first gallery into this hill, and it does not turn its head as the company files past.

choices.label: Walk past it without looking and keep walking.
Look at it properly, once, so you know.

nodes.body: The cutting-shop is where the irons were made: a cold forge, a tally-die still bolted to its anvil, racks of blanks gone entirely to rust. The cutting-orders remain pinned to the bench under a stone. A dwarf smith is folded up beneath the bellows with his tools laid out beside him in careful order.

choices.label: Cut a blank into a ninth iron on the die.
Take the tally-die off the anvil.
Read the cutting-orders on the bench.
Light the forge; you need the heat and the light.

nodes.body: Three hours of cold work on a die that badly wants a striker and a proper smith, with Ilsabet reading the tally-order aloud stroke by stroke while Dellach swings. What comes off the anvil at the end of it is a ninth key-iron that is nine parts correct and one part entirely yours.

choices.label: Take it and go to the door.
Cut a second one while the die is set.

nodes.body: The tally-die comes off the anvil in eleven minutes of work and wraps into forty pounds of dwarf steel that decides what any key-iron says. Ilsabet observes, while lashing it into her pack, that this makes it either the most valuable object in the hill or the most dangerous one. She then observes that it is quite obviously both at once, and stops talking about it.

choices.label: Carry it and go to the door.

nodes.body: The cutting-orders read like any legion requisition until the final clause. Nine irons commissioned at the founding, eight to be cut with the holding tally, and the ninth to be cut with a name left deliberately blank, to be filled in by the hand that would keep the count. The blank, the order says twice, must never be cut a second time.

choices.label: Take the orders and go to the door.

nodes.body: The Ninefold Door stands at the end of everything, dwarf iron set in a frame of much older stone, with nine sockets arranged in a ring. Eight of them are filled and warm. The ninth is empty and worn bright. The metal of the door moves very slightly outward and back on a nine-count, and behind it, patient and enormous, is something that is neither asleep nor awake.
