choices.label: Set the ninth iron in its socket and lock the door.
Draw the eight irons and unmake the Compact.
Take the ninth iron out of the hill entirely.
Open the door a hand's width and look.
Withdraw. This is a Warden matter and a Ledger crime.
Knock, the way you knocked at the gate.
Walk out of the hill and never speak of it again.

nodes.body: Twenty minutes on the first landing with boots off, which the keeper's board warned about in chalk in words of one syllable. The stair's own traffic arrives on schedule and finds a company sitting down in the middle of a right of way that has been in continuous use for nine hundred years.

A token comes out of the second niche, and the seven remaining tokens all turn a quarter turn in their sockets at the same moment. The stair below fills with the sound of somebody coming up two flights at a time in order to correct an error in the arrangement.

The steps are counted aloud in the dark to keep five people together, which works admirably for the first eight numbers. At nine a second voice takes over the counting from somewhere below the company, and continues without any break in the rhythm. Everybody keeps descending, because the numbers keep arriving, and every single one of them is correct.

A hand goes out to take hold of what is passing on the stair, and it turns out to be entirely willing to be held. It has been waiting a considerable time for somebody to initiate the transaction rather than merely submit to it, and it is grateful in its own fashion.

The rope is hauled in hand over hand and comes up cut clean at forty feet, with no scout and no signal on the end of it. The company climbs four hundred steps back to a hillside in daylight, to compose a letter to a fen family about somebody who always went down first.

A hail goes down a dwarf hall in the correct Warden form, and the answer comes back accurately from six directions at once, in six voices the company heard reading a duty roster upstairs. The lamps out in the flooded gallery all turn together toward the foot of the stair.

ending.title: Somebody Down Here Must Be Warden

nodes.body: The ferry is holed from underneath and goes down in eight feet of warm water with its crate still lashed amidships. The crate opens as it sinks, and whatever the Compact had packed into it decides, reasonably enough, that the nearest hands in the water will do perfectly well.

One breath taken, and one look down into warm black water with a lamp held under the surface to see by. The thing that has been turning over below the company for the whole crossing turns over once more, without any hurry at all, in order to look back up.

The broken span of the ledge is taken as a shortcut, on the reasonable assumption that dwarf stone fails slowly and gives warning. It does fail slowly, everywhere except here, where nine hundred years of warm water have been working patiently at the mortar from underneath.

The bound Warden is asked what he is counting toward, and he answers in detail, with dates, in a voice that becomes several voices in the course of the reply. The lamps down the gallery stop their work in order to listen, and the company is still standing in the water when they finish.

The pay-bell is rung once in a deep hall, which is precisely what a pay-bell is for. The garrison answers it: eleven from behind the barracks barricade, the paymaster's clerks up out of the flooded gallery, and all of them forming into the old order to be paid what they are owed.

A search for a dead paymaster's hands succeeds. They are set in the wall's tally-groove where they have been cutting the same nine strokes over and over for eleven years, and they are still working when the lamp finds them, and they stop the moment they are noticed.

Eight key-irons come out of eight warm sockets in under a minute, taken by a company that came here for salvage and stayed for the arithmetic. The Ninefold Door then does exactly what nine hundred years of dwarf engineering, nine irons, and nine hands were arranged to prevent it from doing.

The wall-tally is read down to the bottom of the final group, where the ninth stroke has been begun and then left unfinished halfway. Beside it a name has been cut into the stone in fresh, bright work that has not yet had time to dull. It is not the paymaster's name and it is not Coren Vale's name; it is the name of whoever happens to be reading it.

A lamp breaks against nine hundred years of accounts and the chapel goes up in a light that shows exactly what is sitting on all nine benches. Vale stands in the middle of the fire entirely unharmed, apologising for the inconvenience, and explaining that the tally is not kept on the wall.

A name is spoken aloud in a warm chapel, and Vale writes it into his book without hurry and blots it carefully. The company walks out of the hill four strong and genuinely rich, with the frontier safe for nine more years, and that is a real thing that was really bought, and none of the four can look directly at it.

The captain's own name goes into the ninth hand's book, and the company is sent up the stair with the ledger, the iron, and the back pay. A new keeper sits down at a clerk's desk to learn a count that has been running for nine hundred years and shows no sign whatsoever of finishing.

Coren Vale walks to the Ninefold Door at knifepoint as surety, entirely cooperative and faintly amused by the whole arrangement. On the way he explains, conversationally, that a hostage is only ever worth what the other party is unwilling to lose. The thing behind this door has never been unwilling to lose anything at all, and he has watched it prove that nine times.

A stand is made in a chapel against nine benches of standing dust, and the company wins it for something over ninety seconds. Then it loses, for the reason Vale did not think worth mentioning, which is that everybody who has ever sat down in that room remains on the roll.

The silence after Vale's death is waited out, to learn what a count does when it has no keeper. The answer arrives from the direction of the door within four minutes: it looks for the nearest hand that has held an iron today, and it is not remotely particular about consent.

A ride down the wheel-race on a paddle, to establish where the water actually goes. It goes to a shaft, and then to a sump, and then into a chamber that the dwarves pumped out continuously for nine hundred years for a reason they wrote down in three separate places.

The company stays at the pump, because the deep has to be kept dry and somebody has to do it. Shifts are worked on dwarf machinery for eleven days, and the door business is left for the Wardens, who arrive in spring and find a wheel in excellent order with nobody attending it.

The wheel jams on the captain's word with Kettle and Odd still on the low side of the race. Nine hundred years of held water goes precisely where it has always wanted to go, considerably faster than anybody can climb, and the shouting stops before the water does.

The wheel-race is crossed together and quickly, because the Fenkin crew has seen you and is shouting, which puts two people in the gap at the same moment. The gap between two paddles has always been exactly one person wide, and the wheel does not adjust for enthusiasm.

A ring is taken off the arm of a chair that has no king sitting in it. All nine attendants turn their heads together to see who has accepted the office, and the plaque beneath the ninth chair turns out, on closer reading, to have been a job description all along.

One long look at the occupied chair, taken deliberately, so that at least one person in the company would be able to say what was actually in the room. The thing in the chair returns the courtesy in full, and at considerable length, and by then nobody is leaving.

A dwarf forge is lit for the first time in nine hundred years, because the company wants heat and working light and both are reasonable. The flue runs, as dwarf flues do, straight up into the pay-hall and straight down into the door gallery, announcing the work to everything that has ever worked here.

A second ninth iron is cut on a die whose own written orders state twice that the blank must never be cut a second time. In the space of one hammer stroke the hill's arithmetic acquires a tenth hand, for which it has no socket, no schedule, and no tolerance whatsoever.

Three knocks on the Ninefold Door, since knocking worked so well at the gate. The door answers them: three knocks returned from the other side in exactly the same rhythm, at a scale that brings dust off the ceiling and removes every opinion from everybody present in about two seconds.

Four hundred steps back up, out through the gap in the door, across the moor, and into Gallowmere by the second evening. The report says the vault is unsafe and says nothing else at all, and five people spend the remainder of their lives not talking about the same afternoon.

The door gallery is the last hundred yards, and it is lit: nine niches, nine lamps, all trimmed. The air moves in and out along the floor on a nine-count that everybody has been hearing all day without naming. Halfway along, a pair of Warden's boots stands neatly against the wall with the tags still in them.

choices.label: Walk it, lamps up, and do not stop.
Put out your own lamps and walk it in the dark.
Take the tags out of the boots; somebody's family gets a name.

nodes.body: Two Warden tags are lifted out of a pair of boots that were set down neatly by their owner in a place where nothing at all is neat by accident. The nine lamps of the gallery go out in order from the far end, and the boots turn out, on reflection, to have been a place setting.

The ninth iron goes into the ninth socket, and the socket takes it the way a lock takes its own key, without argument. The door's slow breathing stops in the middle of a count. Eight irons and a ninth, all nine of them warm, the frame taking up the load, and behind it nothing moving at all for the first time in nine hundred years.

choices.label: Break the tally-die so no tenth iron can ever be cut.
Take the keeper's ring; a count still needs a hand.
Get everyone up the stair while it is quiet.
Drive it in crooked so the socket jams forever.

nodes.body: The tally-die is carried back to the cutting-shop and broken across its own anvil in four strokes, and dwarf steel comes apart in a way that dwarf steel is not supposed to come apart. Ilsabet gathers every fragment into a sack afterwards, on her hands and knees, checking the floor twice. She does not trust fragments of anything, and she says so while she is doing it.

choices.label: Go up the stair.

nodes.body: The ninth hand's ring lies on the desk where Vale left it, warm and exactly sized for whoever picks it up next. The arithmetic beside it is not complicated: nine irons will hold the lid without a keeper right up until something outside decides to test the arrangement. A count kept honestly by somebody who hates the work is the entire difference between the two situations.

choices.label: Put it on. Somebody has to keep the count.
Leave it on the desk. Nobody in this company signs that.

nodes.body: The ring goes on, and the count arrives at the back of the skull like a schedule of payments read aloud by a patient clerk. It is not a voice and it is not a compulsion of any kind; it is an obligation, and it is quite specific about dates. The captain of the Ninth Sword stands in a dwarf chapel and understands the shape of the rest of a life.

choices.label: Take the company up the stair.

nodes.body: This is the decision to unmake the Compact, and it deserves saying out loud. Eight irons in eight warm sockets. Nine hundred years of instalments paid by people who were never consulted about any of it. And a company of five standing in front of the only working arrangement anybody has ever managed with the thing on the other side.

choices.label: Draw one iron and watch what the door does.
Draw all eight at once and run.
Draw them, then wedge the ring of sockets with the ninth.
Change your mind and seat the ninth instead.

nodes.body: One iron out, and the door leans a quarter of an inch outward against its frame. Two, and the stone around the sockets begins visibly to sweat. Three, and the door speaks in the paymaster's voice, and asks with genuine courtesy whether the company has come here to settle the account or merely to increase it.

choices.label: Re-seat all three and step back from it.
Keep drawing. Finish what you started.
Ask it what it is owed.

nodes.body: Three irons go back into three sockets, put there by hands that are not remotely steady, and the door settles with a sound like a held breath being let out slowly. The paymaster's voice thanks the company by name, all five names, and pronounces them correctly, and then stops.

choices.label: Get out of the hill.

nodes.body: The ninth iron is driven crosswise through the socket ring rather than into it, dwarf iron biting on dwarf iron until the entire ring is locked into a single piece that no hand can draw and no keeper can ever count. It is crude, and permanent, and in nobody's written orders.

choices.label: Leave it wedged and go up the stair.
Test it first; put your weight on the door.

nodes.body: A hand's width of the Ninefold Door, held open on the poleaxe haft with Dellach's boot braced hard against the frame. Warm air comes out of the gap in a rhythm that is not wind and never was wind at any point today. There is light on the other side of it, and the light is not lamplight, and it has no obvious source anywhere.

choices.label: Look through it.
Put a lamp through first and watch what happens to it.
Shut it again without looking. Nobody needs to know.
Speak through the gap.

nodes.body: Behind the Ninefold Door is not a beast in a lair but a hall the size of the hill, with something at the far end of it too large to resolve into any shape at all. Standing in rows in front of that, in Warden cloaks and Fenkin leather and dwarf mail, are eleven hundred people, and every one of them is counting.

choices.label: Shut it and seat the ninth iron.
Shut it and get out of the hill.
Go in for them. Somebody has to.

nodes.body: A lit lamp is set through the gap on the end of a rope and lowered a foot. It burns steadily for four seconds, then goes out from the wick downward, which is not something lamps do. Then it comes back up the rope, relit by nobody at all, and the colour of the flame is better than it was before.

choices.label: Look through it now that you have to know.
Reach through and take the lamp back.

nodes.body: The door is eased shut on nothing seen and the haft withdrawn, and the count resumes precisely where it left off, without any comment. Five people stand in a dwarf gallery having decided together not to know something that each of them will privately want to know for the rest of their lives.

choices.label: Go up the stair.
Withdraw properly and make it a Warden matter.

nodes.body: The arithmetic works from the other direction too. Eight irons hold the lid for as long as nobody tests it, but the ninth iron is the count itself, and a count that cannot be kept is a debt that cannot be collected. The ninth iron is currently in your pack, wrapped in salt-cloth.

choices.label: Wrap it deep and carry it out of the hill.
Seat it after all; a shut door is worth more than leverage.
Carry it out and sink it in the deepest pool on the moor.
Carry it in the open and let them come and ask for it.

nodes.body: Salt-cloth, then oilcloth, then the middle of the pack, with Ilsabet's chalk marks laid across the flap in two directions. The hill's entire attention arrives and settles on five people who are now, quite formally, in possession of the ninth hand's instrument and walking out of the door with it.

choices.label: Up the stair, and quickly.

nodes.body: The honest option gets said out loud in front of the Ninefold Door, by Nyre, who has been assembling the argument for two days and delivers it in about four sentences. This arrangement is nine hundred years old. It is a Warden matter and a Ledger crime, and a company of five people with one commission does not get to be the hinge of it.

choices.label: Out the way you came in, and no souvenirs.
Out, but take the pay-ledger from the counting room.
Out, and burn the nine gate lamps behind you.
Out, and sell what you know to Corrow instead.

nodes.body: Back up to the counting room for four pounds of paper that the Marshal will read carefully and the Ledger will want burnt. The lamp above the table is still lit, and behind the table the clerk's alcove is exactly as it was, with the plaster tally running all the way up to the ceiling.

choices.label: Take the ledger and go.
Take the ledger and the clerk's tally off the plaster too.

nodes.body: Four hundred steps up, and the hill has revised its opinion of the company. The flights are longer than they were on the way down. The stair-shrine's ninth niche is warm again, all nine lamps in the gallery are lit and trimmed, and at the top of everything the great door has closed to within a thumb's width of shut.

choices.label: Force the great door with everything you have.
Go out up the spoil chute.
Go out by the mason's postern.
Wait for the ninth hour and walk out with the file.
Sit down on the stair. You are finished.

nodes.body: Five people, a poleaxe haft, a Warden's shield used as a fulcrum, and eleven minutes of the worst work anybody in the company has ever done. The door gives an inch at a time against a pressure that is not weight, and is not wind, and is plainly not interested in being negotiated with.

choices.label: Get everyone through the moment it is wide enough.
Hold it and count them through by name.

nodes.body: The spoil chute from below is forty feet of loose scree at an angle that was unpleasant on the way down and is considerably worse now that everybody is tired. The sump behind you is filling steadily and audibly. The lamps in the gallery are going out one at a time, from the far end, working methodically toward the foot of the stair.

choices.label: Go up in pairs, slowly, and take the skin off your hands.
Send the strongest up first to haul the rest.

nodes.body: Out by the mason's postern into weather, with the lead seal broken behind you and the corridor beyond lighting itself politely, one niche at a time, all the way back to the stair. It has the manner of a house showing a guest to the door and watching to see that they leave.

choices.label: Get off the hill.

nodes.body: The ninth hour is waited out in the oil store, and then the file forms on the stair below: nine lamps lifted, the count started, everything on schedule. The Ninth Sword walks out of Kar Duhn in the middle of it with the rhythm right and nobody's hands anywhere they can be seen.

choices.label: Break off at the gate and get clear.
Stay in the file to the end of the count; it is only nine.

nodes.body: The Barrow Moor at dawn, with the hill behind you and Gallowmere half a day ahead. The company carries whatever it decided to carry. Nyre asks the question that has to be settled before anybody speaks to a Warden, which is not what happened, but what it is that you are going to say happened.

choices.label: Straight to Gallowmere and the Marshal.
Two days in a shepherd's bothy first; they are spent.
Put it to the company as a company. All five voices.
Round the town and south with what you carry.

nodes.body: Two days in a shepherd's bothy with a peat fire and no watch to keep between anybody. Kettle sleeps eleven hours without moving. Dellach's hands come back to him by the second evening. Ilsabet writes the entire account down twice in case one copy burns, and by the third morning the company remembers how to behave like people.

choices.label: Walk into Gallowmere on the third morning.

nodes.body: The company council convenes on a wet hillside and runs for an hour. Dellach argues for the Marshal and the written record; Nyre for the Ledger hearing and the naming of Halloway; Kettle for the road south and no names at all. Ilsabet argues for whichever choice keeps the fewest copies of the truth in the fewest hands.

choices.label: Take it to the Marshal, all five names on it.
Take it in and let the record decide it, all five names on it.
Let them argue it out and then decide for yourself.

nodes.body: There is a promise to be kept, made in a lamp gallery in front of witnesses and written down in Nyre's book, and keeping it means going back up a hillside that the company has just spent everything it had in order to leave. Dellach is already checking the postern route without being asked.

choices.label: Go in at the postern and get him out.
Call him out from the gate and wait one hour, no more.
Go in by the great door because it is faster.

nodes.body: Gallowmere in the rain again, and everybody is waiting. The Warden's tower has a lamp in the window; a Ledger coach with southern horses stands outside the counting house; the Rooks are in the muster yard pretending not to watch the gate. At the road shrine a woman is lighting candles, and her son is under that hill.

choices.label: Report to Redd, on the record, in full.
Go to the Ledger hearing and name Halloway.
Write the report the Wardens will read in fifty years.
Go back up the hill for the keeper's boy before anything else.
Tell the boy's mother the truth before you tell anyone else.
Say the minimum, take the fee, and be gone by dark.
Hear Corrow's price for your silence and your maps.

nodes.body: The boy's mother is at the road shrine, and she is told the truth in a wet street by a captain who has been rehearsing the words for two days and gets them wrong regardless. It turns out that she already knew, and had known since midsummer, and that she has been lighting her candles in nines the entire time. She thanks you for coming to her first, which is worse than anything else she could have said.

choices.label: Take her with you to the Marshal.
Stay with her until the candle burns out.

nodes.body: Warden-Marshal Ansel Redd reads it twice, all of it, without asking a single question in the meantime. Then he sets the pages down, squares them, and asks the only three questions that matter to him: what is shut, what is loose, and what exactly is in the company's pack.

choices.label: Ask for the Warden charter and a standing writ.
Hand over the ninth iron with the report.
Keep the iron, and have him write to the Deep Road wardens.
Put Vale's book on the table and let him decide.
Tell him the door is shut and leave the rest out.

nodes.body: The written report will outlive everybody in the room: dated, signed by five hands, sealed into the Warden archive at Gallowmere. It requires the captain of the Ninth Sword to set down in plain words precisely what was done to the Ninefold Door, by whom, and in what order it was done.

choices.label: Write that the company now keeps the count.
Write that the door is open and how far.
Write that three irons were drawn and reseated.
Write that the sockets are wedged and ask for masons.
Write that the company did not go through the door.

nodes.body: The Ledger hearing convenes in the counting room with three factors down from the south, and Halloway sits at the end of the table taking his own minutes in that engraved hand. Nyre stands up as a sister of the Reckoning to say that the account is not what the account says it is.

choices.label: Testify in full, everything, on the record.
Testify, and hand the Ledger the iron as surety.
Withdraw the accusation for what he is offering.

nodes.body: The ninth iron is kept, wrapped, and entered on the record as company property held in trust, which takes Redd's clerk two attempts to phrase. Redd's own letter goes south to the Deep Road wardens over his seal that evening. For the first time in nine hundred years the Compact's count cannot be kept at Kar Duhn. And Vale's book lies open on the Marshal's table at the page that lists eight more doors, with the nearest of them under the mountains at the far end of the Deep Road, and a date written against it that falls this winter.

The writ of salvage is upgraded to a Warden charter with a standing commission and a company seal, and the Ninth Sword is entered in the Marshal's book as a name rather than a hire. The first order issued under it reads, in Redd's own hand: hold the hill, and report the hour of every lamp.

The ledger is delivered, the ninth iron is handed across a Warden's table and locked into a Warden's strongbox, and sixty crowns are paid in full with the hazard added on without any argument at all. There is a door under the Barrow Moor that is shut tonight, and will still be shut in the morning.

Eleven hundred pages of instalments in nine different hands are laid on a Warden-Marshal's desk, which makes them his problem, his career, and no longer the company's business at all. Redd reads the final twenty pages twice over without speaking. He has the slow attention of a man working out that his own predecessor signed one of them.

Factor Halloway is named to his face in front of three southern factors, and Nyre matches the ninth signature against his own order-book in open hearing. He does not deny it, which surprises nobody in the room except the factors. A Ledger house discovers that its frontier accounts have been settled in people for eleven years by a man who kept genuinely excellent records.

A socket ring locked into a single piece by a ninth iron driven crosswise, reported in plain words and copied out twice for the archive. A Warden request goes south the same week for masons and a mining engineer at Warden expense. What the company did cannot be undone by any hand, and cannot be trusted indefinitely by anybody who understands how old metal ages.

The promise is kept. In by the postern at dusk, the lamp gallery empty and all nine lamps lit, and the boy found asleep in the oil store where he had been hiding for two days on half a loaf. He goes out over Dellach's shoulder into weather that has never felt better to anybody.

A short honest report that says the door is shut and stops there, and the fee is paid, and the company is thanked and released. Four people each know that a decision was taken in a dwarf gallery to leave nine hundred years of arithmetic out of a Warden's file, and none of them raises it again.

The ninth iron is handed to the Ledger as surety and entered in its register under a number, which makes it the safest place on the frontier and also the one place the Compact has always been able to reach. The company keeps a receipt that will be worth exactly what the paper is worth.

It goes into a Warden file in the captain's own hand: the door is shut, all nine irons are seated, and the count is kept by the captain of the Ninth Sword. There will be a visit to Gallowmere every ninth night for the rest of a life that now has a schedule attached to it.

The truth is entered in the record to the inch. The tower is emptied within the hour, the evacuation order is posted by noon, and a company that did the honest thing sits in the muster yard watching a frontier town load its carts on account of a hand's width of open door.

Three irons drawn and reseated, written down exactly in those words, and a Warden clerk copies it out twice while Redd asks the question nobody in the room is able to answer. Whether a socket that has been emptied once holds the same as a socket that has never been emptied at all.

The file records that the company reached the Ninefold Door, described it accurately, touched nothing at all, and came back out again. It is the most defensible sentence anywhere in the Warden archive at Gallowmere. It is also the one that the Ninth Sword will be asked about in every taproom on the frontier for the next nine years.

Sixty crowns for the ledger, with no questions invited and none asked by anybody in the tower, and the company is out through the gate before dark with the money split five ways. Nobody says anything much on the road south for the first day. There is an understanding between them, never once spoken aloud, that whatever lies under that hill is now somebody else's arithmetic.

The maps, the route, the lamp hours and the company's silence are sold to the Rooks for two hundred crowns and a promise. In spring the Rooks go up to Kar Duhn with eleven people, and nobody at all comes back down to complain about the price that was agreed.

Gallowmere is skirted at a distance and the Ledger road is taken south with the pack still packed. No report, no fee, no charter, and a ninth iron travelling further from its socket every day in the luggage of five people who have agreed, in some detail, never to discuss it.

An argument on a wet hillside is allowed to run until it stops being an argument and becomes a settlement. Kettle goes south that same afternoon with her share and her own opinion of the captain. Nyre returns to her order, Dellach walks into the tower alone with his version of events, and the Ninth Sword ends not in a vault but in a disagreement about paperwork.

An afternoon in a road shrine with a woman lighting candles in nines, which is the right place for a captain to be and entirely the wrong place for this particular captain today. Redd waits until the fourth hour and then writes in his file that the company did not present itself.

The ninth iron is hammered in at an angle to jam the socket permanently, and it works. It also cracks the stone collar around the socket, and a ring of nine that has held for nine hundred years discovers, all at once, that it is now a ring of eight and one wound.

Eight irons are pulled in well under a minute, and the company runs for a stair that is four hundred steps long. It is a plan that requires the door to open slowly. The Ninefold Door has been waiting nine hundred years for the opportunity and sees no reason at all to be slow about it.

The fourth iron is drawn while the paymaster's voice is still being courteous about the state of the account, and then the fifth is drawn as well. After that no further decisions are required of anybody standing in the gallery. The arrangement the dwarves engineered has concluded, and the accounts are being settled in the order in which they were originally opened.

The question is asked through three empty sockets, and it is answered in full, itemised, with dates and running totals. The figure is one that the company is standing inside of. The door explains, without any heat whatsoever, that a debt does not require the consent of the instalment.

A shoulder is put against a wedged door to establish whether the work holds, which it does, entirely, and would have gone on doing. In the same second the thing on the other side puts its own weight against the same door, out of what can only reasonably be described as curiosity.

One sentence is spoken through a hand's width of open Ninefold Door, in common speech, quite politely. The reply does not arrive as sound. It arrives as arithmetic: the company counted, priced, scheduled, and entered against an instalment that is recorded as falling due immediately.

The door is pushed wide and five people walk into a hall the size of a hill to bring out eleven hundred who are standing in rows, counting. It is the most defensible decision anybody makes in this entire story. It adds five to the rows, and changes nothing else at all.

An arm goes through the gap to take back a lamp that has been relit by nobody. The lamp is handed over properly, into the hand that reached for it, by something that has been waiting nine hundred years for a transaction it did not itself have to begin.

The ninth iron is sunk in eleven feet of black water in the middle of the Barrow Moor, which solves the problem for exactly one winter. Then the frost lifts the peat, and a fen-runner's boy finds a strip of warm metal in a drained pool and sells it in Gallowmere for two coppers.

The ninth iron is carried openly across the Barrow Moor as an invitation, on the theory that whatever wants it will have to come out into daylight and negotiate for it. On the second night the company discovers that it does not have to come out at all, and never has.

Nine lamps are smashed and burning in the gate arch as a gesture on the way out, which feels entirely justified at the time. The hill's answer does not arrive that night. It arrives nine nights later, in Gallowmere, in a file that comes up the causeway at the third hour with its own lamps and its own list.

Everything the company learned under the hill is sold to Vasse Corrow in a wet muster yard for good coin and no receipt of any kind. The commission goes back to the tower unfulfilled, with an excuse that Redd does not believe and cannot disprove. A Rooks banner goes up the causeway a week later with eleven people beneath it who were told the easy version.

The plaster tally is chiselled off the alcove wall on the grounds that it is evidence, and evidence is what wins arguments with Wardens. The work takes eleven minutes from first stroke to last. That is about eight minutes longer than the clerk's own arrangement allowed for with whatever it is that comes to read his wall on the hour.

A captain sits down on the two hundredth step because the legs have finished arguing about it. The company will not leave without its captain, which is the entire point of a company. The stair has been getting longer all evening, and it is in no hurry whatsoever.

The great door is held on a shield-fulcrum while five names are called through it in order, which is precisely the arrangement that the shield's dead owner scratched a warning about on its inside face. The fifth name is answered from behind the door, in the captain's own voice, with the correct inflection.

The strongest goes up the chute first to haul the others, which puts one set of hands at the top and four sets of boots on forty feet of scree that has been waiting all day for a reason to move. It moves while the sump behind them is still filling.

The file is stayed with to the end of the count, because it is only nine, and the rhythm is easy, and the company is very nearly out. The ninth number arrives on the causeway in open air with the moor plainly visible, and the count starts again from one without any gap at all.

The great door is taken because it is faster, and because the boy needs an hour of daylight to walk out in. The door is wide enough for one person going quickly, and then it is not wide enough for anybody at all. The company keeps its promise as far as the threshold and no further than that, and Nyre writes down the hour.

Kettle's report from the causeway proves accurate in every particular, as her reports generally do. The Rooks are in the yard, a Ledger coach stands outside the counting house, and eleven Warden cloaks on the gate do not fit the men wearing them. The company walks into Gallowmere regardless, because there is nowhere else on this frontier left to walk to.

ending.title: Who Was Waiting at the Gate

nodes.body: The causeway into Gallowmere, in rain that has not stopped since the company left it. The stockade ahead, the tower lamp burning at an hour that means somebody is waiting up, and a coach with southern horses standing outside the counting house with its curtains drawn and its driver still on the box.

choices.label: Walk in openly, up the middle, in your own colours.
Send Kettle ahead to see who is waiting at the gate.
Go round to the Ledger's back gate and be quiet about it.

nodes.body: Kettle is back from the gate inside eleven minutes with a scout's list, delivered flat and in order of importance. The Rooks are in the muster yard doing nothing, badly, in the rain. A Ledger clerk is taking names at the counting house door, and there are eleven Warden cloaks on the gate that do not remotely fit the men currently inside them.

choices.label: Walk in anyway; there is nowhere else to walk.
Wait for full dark and go in over the stockade.

nodes.body: The Warden's anteroom, with wet cloaks steaming on the pegs and the report copied fair in Ilsabet's hand. You read it through once more while a clerk pretends not to watch the pack that has not left the captain's shoulder since the hill, and has not been set down anywhere at all.

choices.label: Go in and give it to Redd straight.
Ask for the Ledger factor to be present when you speak.
Leave the fair copy with the clerk and walk out of town.

nodes.body: A fair copy of everything is left on a clerk's desk with the company's five names on it and no witness to the handing over of it. Redd reads it eleven days later, by which time the coach with the southern horses has been back to the counting house twice and left again.
